name: Hot spring
notes: Geothermal ground: colour-banded thermophile microbial mats in the runoff channels, heat-tolerant mosses and grasses on warm ground, and specialist wetland plants where the water cools. Drawn on Yellowstone, Iceland (Hveravellir, Reykjadalur), New Zealand (Rotorua) and Japanese onsen valleys.

growth.juvenile_note: Tiny two-winged nutlets sprout in early summer on moss, bare soil or burnt ground. Seedlings have minute round cotyledons, then small, downy, coarsely toothed, rounded leaves on hairy reddish twigs. At the treeline the young tree soon sprouts extra stems from its base, becoming a crooked, multi-stemmed bush with dark reddish-brown bark that whitens and peels only on older stems.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings usually come up in tight clumps of 5-30 from a forgotten rodent seed cache. Each has two small oval cotyledons, then tiny wedge-shaped leaves with three teeth at the tip, grey-green above and woolly-white below, on one thin stem. The taproot races ahead while the top grows slowly; after some years it branches into a stiff, twiggy, rounded grey-green shrub.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Purshia tridentata (seed needs 4-6 wk chilling at 2 C; seed-bearing at 8-10 yr; plants of 115 and 128 yr; usually 0.9-1.2 m, up to 4.5 m; shade intolerant; natural regeneration mostly from rodent caches); Wikipedia (1-5 m; leaves 5-20 mm, 3-5-lobed)

growth.juvenile_note: Germinates on wet mud or in shallow water: a hair-like shoot, then 2-4 tiny leaves and 2-6 ribbon leaves floating flat on the water before stiff, erect, flat grey-green leaves rise. By the end of its first summer a seedling is 60-85 cm tall and has sent rhizomes out into a clump up to 3 m across. Each shoot lives about a year; the clone persists for decades.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Typha latifolia): germinates best at 25-30 C in high light; 2-4 small then 2-6 floating leaves before erect ones; seedlings 60-85 cm after 84 d; flowers early in 2nd year; ramets die within a year, rhizomes live about 2 yr; one seedling's rhizomes spread 3 m in a season; shade intolerant.

ground.name: Dwarf swan-neck moss

growth.juvenile_note: Spreads mostly by its brittle shoot tips and tiny buds that break off and blow about; on warm, steaming ground a fragment puts out green threads and short upright shoots of narrow, long-pointed leaves. These pack into a soft, yellowish-green turf; next to the vents, where nothing else can grow, it forms a continuous short mossfield.
growth.source: Given, vegetation of the Taupo Volcanic Zone geothermal fields (Campylopus pyriformis mossfield, mean height 5 cm, on ground 44 C at 10 cm; with Kunzea tenuicaulis on 50 C ground); Smith, Moss Flora of Britain and Ireland (turfs, deciduous shoot tips); rates estimated.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

Smith, Moss Flora of Britain and Ireland; Landcare Research, Naturally uncommon ecosystems: fumaroles.

ground.name: Hot springs panic grass

growth.juvenile_note: Like all Dichanthelium it starts as a flat winter rosette of short, broad, softly hairy leaves pressed to the warm ground. In spring it sends up leafy stems with small open panicles; later in the season side branches carry smaller leaves and hidden self-pollinating flowers. On geothermal soil roots grow in ground at 40-57 C, helped by a fungus living in the plant.
growth.source: Stout & Al-Niemi, Heat-tolerant flowering plants of active geothermal areas in Yellowstone National Park (Annals of Botany 2002); Redman et al., Thermotolerance generated by plant/fungal symbiosis (Science 2002); Flora of North America (Dichanthelium life cycle); ages estimated.

repro.note: spring flowers open; later autumn branches carry closed, self-pollinating flowers

ground.source: Dichanthelium lanuginosum (Elliott) Gould, hot springs panic grass: small softly hairy rosette panic grass, the commonest flowering plant on hot geothermal soil in Yellowstone (roots at 40-57 C, with the fungal endophyte Curvularia protuberata); also widespread on ordinary dry ground across North America. Kew POWO (accepted); Stout & Al-Niemi 2002; Redman et al. 2002.

By May-June it carries tiny, narrow, purplish panicles on stems 5-20 cm, then yellows and dies by July as summer heat bakes the crust.

Culms 5-20 cm (batch). Germination days and growth fractions estimated.

ground.name: Maidenhair fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores germinate in about 6 days; heart-shaped green prothalli a few mm across form in 1-2 months on wet rock or soil, then two-leaved fernlets appear: tiny single fan-shaped leaflets on hair-thin black stalks. Later fronds branch into many wedge-shaped, pale-green leaflets and the creeping rhizome spreads a lacy mat over seeps and damp walls.
growth.source: Spore culture study, Not Sci Biol 9(4) 2017 (germination from day 6, heart-shaped gametophytes at 27-60 d, then two-leaved fernlets); clump growth, spore age and rhizome life estimated from growers and genus habit
